subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: joining because friends are going [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Anirban, and I was standing two rows behind Abhinav at the rally. On Friday he had said, “Everyone from tuition is going, so I'm going,” and when I asked what the march wanted, he shrugged and laughed. Today he waved a paper flag at strangers. Then the crowd near the barricade began shoving, and somebody shouted that the road was closing. Abhinav's laugh stopped. “Which way is the gate?” he asked me. I didn't know either; neither of us had checked. He grabbed his friend's sleeve and we pushed sideways for ten minutes, his water bottle gone and his phone nearly dead. I can't say what he felt, but he kept muttering, “What are we even here for?” Finally a shopkeeper let us sit inside, and Abhinav rang his mother from the shop.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav go to the rally?
qa.a: Everyone from tuition was going, so he went too.

qa.q: What might Abhinav have been feeling when he asked which way the gate was?
qa.a: Fear and confusion: his laugh stopped and he kept asking what they were there for, which suggests he did not know what he was supporting or how to leave.

qa.q: What could Abhinav have done before going, and why would it help?
qa.a: He could have found out what the march demanded and agreed a leaving route and a check-in with a parent, because then he would know what he was backing and how to get out.

qa.q: How does the day look to Anirban, who tagged along?
qa.a: Anirban was pulled into the same confusion with no exit plan either, and could only guess at Abhinav's feelings while trying to find a safe way out.

grounding: A teen joins a protest because friends do, without knowing the demands, and is lost when tension rises.

subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: joining because friends are going [Pitfall]
passage:
Saturday morning: Ankita's message lit up the group chat: "Everyone's going to the march at 4!! Lalremsiami you HAVE to come." Lalremsiami didn't know what the march was about. Something about the university. But all six of her friends were going, and the photos would be everywhere. She said yes.

Saturday, 5 pm: The crowd at the square was bigger than she'd imagined. People were chanting slogans she didn't understand. When someone handed her a placard, she held it without reading it. Then shouting started near the front, and the crowd pushed backward. She lost Ankita. She didn't know which street led out.

Sunday: She'd found a lane, called her mother and got home safely, shaken. At breakfast her father asked what the march had been for. She opened her mouth and realised she couldn't say. "I just went because everyone did," she said quietly.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel when the crowd pushed back and she lost Ankita?
qa.a: She felt frightened and confused, not knowing which street led out.

qa.q: What would you change first before joining any gathering?
qa.a: Find out what it is about and who is organising it, tell a parent, and agree with friends on a meeting point and a way out if things get tense.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami's parents have felt when she called from the lane?
qa.a: They were probably alarmed and worried, and then relieved that she had found a lane and called.

grounding: Shows a teen joining a march out of excitement and fear of missing out without knowing its demands, then being lost and unclear when tensions rise.

passage:
Yamini, you want to go to that rally just because your friends are going? Let me tell you what your Tushar mama did at fifteen.

It was in Nagpur. My whole cricket team was going to some procession near the railway station. I didn't know what it was about. I only knew everyone was going and I didn't want to be the one left out.

So I went. There were flags, drums, slogans in a language half of us didn't speak. Somebody gave me a banner. I was proud to carry it, till an old man asked me what it meant. I couldn't answer.

Then the police arrived, and people started running. My friends scattered. I hid in a tea stall for an hour, shaking, with no idea how to get home.

When I finally did, your nani asked, "What were you marching for?" I couldn't say.

qa.q: Where did young Tushar hide when people started running?
qa.a: In a tea stall for an hour.

qa.q: How did young Tushar feel when the old man asked what the banner meant?
qa.a: Young Tushar felt embarrassed and exposed, realising there was no idea behind the banner he carried.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have changed how the day went?
qa.a: If he had asked what the procession was for before going, he could have decided properly and planned how to get home safely.

qa.q: How might Tushar's friends on the cricket team have felt when everyone scattered?
qa.a: They were probably frightened and confused too, since they had also gone along without a plan or a meeting point.

grounding: An elder recalls joining a procession because friends were going, without knowing its demands, and having no clarity or way out when tensions rose.
